story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I posted AgentOS here a few months ago. Back then, it was pretty amazing to see what these agents can do and I'm improved it a lot since then.

The biggest change is that it's built for my phone now. I start work at my desk, walk away, and check on it or answer an agent from my phone over Tailscale. Chat sessions run in their own process, so restarting the server doesn't kill a turn that's halfway done.

It also runs tasks now. You give it a prompt, it makes a git worktree, the agent works there and opens a PR, and I review it later. Each workspace can have an orchestrator that starts tasks, reviews the PRs and merges the ones that pass CI and a review of that exact commit. Anything risky comes to me as an ask that needs Face ID to approve.

It supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Aider, Cursor CLI, Amp and Pi. It's still free and all self-hosted.

npm install -g @saadnvd1/agent-os

https://github.com/saadnvd1/agent-os

I'd love feedback and as I'm sure there will be issues, please share them! Also, if you want to build your own, just fork it. It's all free.

story_text.value:
Author here. Bees is an agentic harness that runs on your own machine — macOS, Windows and Linux, MIT/Apache 2.0.

The problem we kept hitting in client work: every agent platform wanted to be the place your documents live. We wanted the opposite — the orchestrator reads your files in place, on your disk, and we never see them.

How it works: you describe work in plain English, Bees proposes the agents, stages, tools and schedule, and nothing runs until you apply it. Agents execute locally in their own run folders. A separate reviewer agent checks output before it advances a stage. Agents stop and ask for approval before external side effects like sending mail.

Coordination is deliberately thin. In a Regular org we sync team membership, process runs and stages, work claims, and file names with relative paths. Not contents. If you want no third party at all, pick a local model and local tools and it runs fully offline.

Model routing is BYO: local models, your own API keys, or the official Claude Code CLI you already have installed and signed into as yourself. We don't intermediate credentials and we add no per-token or per-run fee — that's the whole point.

Rough edges, honestly: {name the two weakest things — I'd lead with whatever your beta testers actually complained about}. Scripted installers exist but Linux distro coverage is the thinnest. Very happy to answer architecture questions, and I'd particularly like pushback from anyone running multi-machine setups.

Repo: https://github.com/Bees-bot/bees-desktop/

story_text.value:
A friend and I built this for our own calls and are sharing it as is. The itch: we kept copy-pasting Granola transcripts into Claude mid-call, and wondered what would happen if the agent just joined.

Two-minute demo: https://youtu.be/XhCSRiiL67A

How it works: a local Electron app joins the Meet in its own browser as a participant. Your agent drives it over MCP (or HTTP): tools to listen, speak, and write to a shared whiteboard. Any MCP agent works; we built for Claude Code first, and Codex and Cursor run it too. It is your actual session, on your machine, in your repo, with your skills, so it can do real work during the call instead of summarizing afterwards.

The hack: by default it does no speech recognition of its own. It reads Meet's live captions, and speaks through a virtual microphone. This is cheap and surprisingly good! (There is also an experimental realtime mode in app preferences that puts OpenAI's speech-to-speech model in the voice seat, with your agent feeding it facts.)

Bring an ElevenLabs key for a better voice. Works with Google Meet and Slack huddles today; Zoom is in progress. Known issues are in the README.

Try it in your next Google Meet and surprise a friend. Let us know what you think!

story_text.value:
Claude has a way of talking. Most people I work with are tired of it, me included. Call it Claude-speak.

It opens with "Great question" and a header. The answer hides in the middle. It reaches for a metaphor when a plain phrase would do: "a 3,000-line merge gets a skim and a prayer". It explains with a contrast instead of a reason: "this is intent, not behavior". It drops a slogan: "the decision is the feature". It recaps what it just did. It ends with "happy to dig further if useful". An engineering question gets 500 to 600 words of this.

Terse is 22 writing rules as a forced output style. First sentence is the answer. One idea per sentence. A number or a name in every claim. No slogans, no reframes, no closing offers. 150 words, unless you ask for a document. A hook re-sends a short digest with every prompt, so the rules hold at turn 30.

Same 20 prompts, same codebase, with and without the plugin: Opus 5.5 went from 9,705 words to 4,468 at 32% lower cost. Fable 5.1 wrote 46% fewer words. One prompt in the README: 636 words before, 180 after.

One rule failed. A ban on first person passed every benchmark and lost in daily use. Half my real replies still said "I'll tell you when the compile finishes". The benchmark never asked Claude to act as an agent. Details in docs/benchmark.md.

Claude plugin directory, search "terse". Or /plugin marketplace add lowenbjer/claude-terse. MIT. If it still writes Claude-speak, post the reply as an issue. There's a template.

story_text.value:
Hi, HackerNews!

I'm Samy, co-founder of Allchemy Labs. We built Aether, an MCP server that enables engineers to check for, understand, and fix web accessibility issues all from their IDE. Your preferred coding agent can leverage Aether to open a webpage, scan it using axe-core and return a short, prioritized list of violations along with code fixes or guidance. Every suggested fix is re-tested in a real browser before you see it, and once you apply it, your agent can re-scan the page to verify it worked. You never need to open a browser, use multiple tools, or be an expert in WCAG criteria.

Aether uses our own custom ontology architecture to provide grounded insights to any WCAG violations the scanner finds. Every WCAG technique the engine cites must pass our quality gate. Specifically, it must satisfy the violated success criterion, apply to that kind of element, and remediate that axe rule. If nothing passes, our engine will abstain rather than guess.

We compared Aether against standalone coding agent on its own (Opus 5, 30 anonymized live sites, 111 targets). While the results were mixed we have published the results especially calling out specific wins and improvement opportunities for our insight engine. Read the study here: https://allchemylabs.substack.com/p/we-tested-our-own-access...

Try Aether today, no signup needed. npx -y @allchemylabs/aether-wcag-scanner (any MCP client: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex…) Claude Code plugin: /plugin marketplace add https://github.com/allchemylabs/claude-plugins.git then /plugin install aether-wcag-scanner@allchemylabs Without a key you get the browser scan, local template fixes and verification. A free beta key adds the cloud engine: https://beta.allchemylabs.ai/?src=hn

Feedback from people who have used accessibility scanners and/or suggestion engines would be highly valuable to us, as we aim to build a tool that solves real problems and makes people's lives easier.

Happy to answer any questions and hope to hear from you.

Note: Right now Aether only checks WCAG 2.1 AA. Sites behind bot protection (e.g. Cloudflare challenges) return a "blocked" result instead of a fake scan, so point it at localhost or staging.

story_text.value:
I turned Andrej Karpathy’s tips on understanding LLM output into an Open Source Agent Skill : [make-it-click](https://github.com/ajithraghavan/make-it-click)

Inspired by his X post : as Models do more of the work, we spend more time understanding it. So the format of an answer matters

The Skill picks the simplest format that makes an idea click, and moves up only when needed :

    Clear writing in ASD-STE100 style (strict, 80%, or light)
    Diagrams
    Interactive HTML pages
    Narrated explainer videos (3b1b style)
Bonus : an oversight mode for reviewing Agent work (what changed -> why -> risk -> what to check)

MIT licensed. Works with Claude.ai and Claude Code

https://github.com/ajithraghavan/make-it-click

Inspired by @karpathy: [https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479]

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I was frustrated with expiring credits, subscriptions and generally BS approach in image&video generation space (which is now universally useful and basically a commodity) so I've built Azurade, a hosted service where you have 35+ models (Veo3.1, Seedance 2.5, Wan 3.0, Nano Banana, GPT Image2.5 etc.) behind one non-expiring, fully agent native balance. I care about billing, that's why credits are prepaid and never expire, a failed generation is refunded automatically, and you can buy a pack without a subscription. I got tired of monthly credits (or usage) that vanish at the end of the month

This post is mainly about it's remote MCP server, because that's how I and my friends mostly use it now (via Claude or Codex)

You can add https://azurade.com/mcp in Claude or Codex (or claude code), sign in once through OAuth and the LLM will be able to generate / get all info about models and account / upload files and all that.

I've ran it through oblivious evaluator agent for 8 times to reach good agent ergonomics. After all, if I want to build an agent-native service the users (agent) should evaluate and correct it. Please feel free to point your agents at it and send me the nitpicks and gotchas they encounter. Humans are also welcome :)

Demo video (1m40s, cute dog included): https://youtu.be/tX29WLffXCk

P.S. the stack is Go and Pocketbase, official GO MCP SDK, and the frontend is statically rendered NextJS. The access token is an API key named after the client, so revoking an agent means deleting that key on your profile page. It also works like REST API with an OpenAPI spec.

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I'm the founder of Tofu, a code deployment platform built for agents. Paste our setup prompt to any agent you're already using and Tofu enables your agent to take your project from code to production. Current features include frontend & backend hosting (created & managed by Tofu), Postgres database (created & managed by Tofu), domain management (one-click setup for Cloudflare managed domains, manual DNS record for others), authentication, Google login, and Analytics.

We built Tofu out of our personal frustrations: we're engineers who know how to code, we've deployed live products and understand the process, and our AI agents have already finished writing the code that works locally, yet taking a product fully online still took 2-3 hours: - Setup hosting, backend, database - Copy-pasting a lot of apikeys/secrets from here to there - Setting up correct redirect urls from places to places - Managing DNS records, domains - Setting up a lot services (email, 3rd parth OAuth, etc) - Payments

Tofu works with any MCP-compatible agents, and here's a list of tested agents (10+ different projects end-to-end deployment via Tofu): local coding agents (Claude Code, Codex/ChatGPT, Kimi Code, DSH, Cursor), Instinct, Muse, Kimi Code cloud.

None of that is hard, but each of these services have their own providers and it involves managing 5-10 different accounts. Most cloud providers have their own CLI, but it only works within their own platform and the process still involves a lot of manual interventions. Agents can call any API and use CLIs, but cannot open a Google Cloud project or put a card on file with 5 vendors.

We think deployment is not a compute problem, but an accounts problem. Our endgoal is to utilize SSO across services, and provide agents the ability to deploy a live product end-to-end. We don't want to compete with any cloud providers, but to make agents actually capable of shipping "live" products. We're rolling out features to support buy domains directly from Tofu (we're an authorized reseller of Name.com), and provide more customizability to tech stacks.

We're still very early and have just launched our product, please send us any feedbacks, comments, and we promise we will respond to every single one of them.

story_text.value:
Inspired by games like "super monkey ball" and good 'ol "marble blast".. PolyRoll is basically their evil clone..

Uses a combo of "three.js" and "cannon-es"

--------- Backstory: ---------

3 months ago I stopped at my buddy's house.. he showed me his Claude-code setup.. I had never tried agentic coding so I figured, why not try to make a game?

After some brainstorming and developing a plan with gemini-pro, we set sonnet off on his merry way and went for a swim... About an hour or two later we had a working game (though it was't great, buggy)... After some more prompts to kill the bugs, tweak the play-feel and camera physics- we did some mobile optimizations, added the animations, and designed a d-pad by sending sonnet a photo mockup of the custom buttons we wanted...

For a game made in the span of about 6-8 hours total, it's not bad! Quite difficult/ frustrating at times though.. Some levels get glitchy, and we left it kinda messy/low-poly on purpose!

I don't think my friend has much interest in developing the game further, and I don't have Claude-code, so I figured why not post the game here now so others may enjoy...

---- NOTE: ----

The levels are entirely procedurally generated, no two levels are ever the same...

If you get stuck on a level just reload, you may get easier levels at the expense of starting the game over at level 1 (sorry no saves).. technically infinite, but the levels get very difficult!

Good luck have fun!

hits.story_text:
Inspired by games like "super monkey ball" and good 'ol "marble blast".. PolyRoll is basically their evil clone..

Uses a combo of "three.js" and "cannon-es"

--------- Backstory: ---------

3 months ago I stopped at my buddy's house.. he showed me his Claude-code setup.. I had never tried agentic coding so I figured, why not try to make a game?

After some brainstorming and developing a plan with gemini-pro, we set sonnet off on his merry way and went for a swim... About an hour or two later we had a working game (though it was't great, buggy)... After some more prompts to kill the bugs, tweak the play-feel and camera physics- we did some mobile optimizations, added the animations, and designed a d-pad by sending sonnet a photo mockup of the custom buttons we wanted...

For a game made in the span of about 6-8 hours total, it's not bad! Quite difficult/ frustrating at times though.. Some levels get glitchy, and we left it kinda messy/low-poly on purpose!

I don't think my friend has much interest in developing the game further, and I don't have Claude-code, so I figured why not post the game here now so others may enjoy...

---- NOTE: ----

The levels are entirely procedurally generated, no two levels are ever the same...

If you get stuck on a level just reload, you may get easier levels at the expense of starting the game over at level 1 (sorry no saves).. technically infinite, but the levels get very difficult!

Good luck have fun!
